fixes.explanation: A sheep is a living creature that can run, but Job doesn't mention one here. He says windblown leaf and dry chaff, two things the wind pushes around (Job 13:25). I think Job is showing how small he feels.

Job says to God, “For You record bitter accusations against me and bequeath to me the iniquities of my youth.” (Job 13:26) Bequeath is a fancy word for passing something down, like an inheritance. So Job feels like he's been handed a pile of old mistakes. I think that's a heavy thing to carry around.

Job does say it, so this one is true. He says to God, “For You record bitter accusations against me and bequeath to me the iniquities of my youth.” (Job 13:26) The wording is fancy, so it's easy to doubt.

Job says, “Like a flower, he comes forth, then withers away…” (Job 14:2) Picture a flower on the counter that looks great and then droops. Job uses that picture for a person's life. Up it comes, and then it fades.

Flowers multiplying would be a nice twist, like a batch of dough that doubles itself while I'm not looking. But Job doesn't say that. The flower comes forth, then withers away (Job 14:2). He uses it for a person's life.

Job doesn't ask for extra days. He says the days are determined and God has set limits he cannot exceed (Job 14:5). So he asks God to look away from him and let him rest (Job 14:6) inside those limits. It's a smaller ask than you might expect.

Job says, “…at the scent of water it will bud and put forth twigs like a sapling.” (Job 14:9) Just a whiff, and the old stump gets going. I know folks who perk up at the scent of a fresh batch of cookies. Same energy.

Pruning is careful work, but Job doesn't mention a farmer. It's the scent of water that makes the tree bud (Job 14:9). His picture is a stump and a whiff of water. Job names the water and leaves it there.

A name is a nice thing to keep track of, but Job doesn't bring one up here. He says God would count his steps but would not keep track of his sin (Job 14:16). Sin is the word Job uses. His name never comes into it.

Job says, “…You would cover over my iniquity.” (Job 14:17) He also says his transgression would be sealed in a bag. Both pictures are of sin tucked away, not put on display. I think it's a hopeful thing to hear from him.

Showing it off is the reverse of Job's picture. His transgression is sealed in a bag, and God would cover over his iniquity (Job 14:17). Think how it feels when your worst moment gets passed around the office. Job pictures the opposite of that.

Job says, “…so You destroy a man’s hope.” (Job 14:19) Water wears away the stones and torrents wash away the soil, and he sets God's action beside those. This is a heavy line, friend. I think it comes from a painful place.
Pride isn't the thing in this line. Job says that as water wears away stones, so God destroys a man's hope (Job 14:19). The water and the stones are his picture for it. Hope is what gets destroyed.
